The Visigoths were a Germanic people who became the dominant power in the Iberian Peninsula after the Western Roman Empire's collapse, ruling Spain and Portugal from the fifth to eighth centuries. Their most infamous moment came when Alaric I sacked Rome in 410, one of the most shocking violations of the empire's sanctity and a symbolic marker of Rome's decline. The Visigoths settled primarily in southern Gaul and the Iberian Peninsula after being displaced from Italy by the Ostrogoths and Huns. Under Leovigild, they expanded their territory and consolidated power, though they struggled with religious conflict between Catholic and Arian factions. The Visigothic Code, or Liber Iudiciorum, was an early legal synthesis blending Roman law with Germanic custom, and it served as a model for medieval European law. The Visigoths also produced remarkable scholarship and preserved much classical learning during their reign, a legacy evident in the work of Isidore of Seville. Yet internal civil war and succession disputes weakened the kingdom in the early eighth century, making it vulnerable to outside conquest. Their kingdom fell to rapid Muslim invasion in 711; it fragmented and Christian remnants retreated to the north, beginning the centuries-long conflict known as the Reconquista. Their rule over Iberia lasted longer than any other Germanic kingdom's dominion over its territory, but when it ended, it ended suddenly and completely.
